lesson.title: A Network of Networks: How the Internet Was Built to Survive
lesson.summary: Explains how the internet works as an interconnection of independently run networks held together by TCP/IP, and distinguishes the internet's decentralized routing from the mostly centralized services built on top of it.
lesson.body:
The internet is not one network. It is, as the name suggests, an interconnection of thousands of separately owned and operated networks, run by internet service providers, universities, corporations, and governments, all agreeing to use a common set of protocols so that traffic can pass between them. When you load a webpage, your data typically crosses several of these independently managed networks before reaching its destination, using the packet-based approach and shared protocol rules described in the previous chapter.

The core protocol suite that makes this possible is called TCP/IP. The Internet Protocol, IP, is responsible for addressing, giving every device a numerical address so packets know where to go, and for routing those packets across intermediate networks toward that address. The Transmission Control Protocol, TCP, sits on top of IP and handles reliability: it breaks a message into packets, numbers them, confirms they arrived, and requests any that were lost, so the application using it can treat the connection as a dependable stream of data even though the underlying network is only making a best effort with each individual packet.

This design traces back to the internet's early predecessor, ARPANET, funded by a U.S. Department of Defense research agency in the late 1960s. A frequently repeated claim is that ARPANET was built specifically to survive a nuclear attack; the more accurate history is that its designers, aware of broader Cold War era concerns about network resilience, deliberately avoided a single central hub in favor of a design where packets could be rerouted around failed connections, so no single point of failure could take down the whole network. Whatever the exact motivation, the practical result was a network built for resilience through decentralization at the routing layer, even though, as later chapters explore, resilience at the routing layer does not automatically mean decentralization at every other layer built on top of it.

On top of TCP/IP sit other protocols suited to specific tasks: the Domain Name System, DNS, translates a human-readable website name into the numerical IP address a computer actually needs, functioning something like a phone book. HTTP and HTTPS govern how web browsers and web servers exchange pages, with the "S" indicating the connection is encrypted, a topic covered in detail in the chapters on encryption ahead.

It is worth being precise here, in the spirit of a skeptic's guide: the internet's routing is genuinely decentralized in the sense that no single organization controls all the networks or all the paths packets can take. But many of the services people actually use on top of that infrastructure, search engines, social platforms, banks, are not decentralized at all. The next two chapters draw that distinction sharply, starting with the dominant model for how most applications are actually built.
